To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
paraventricual hypothalamic neurons project to trigeminal sensory neurons and modulate their activities.

the hypothalamic paraventricular nuclei (PVN) are a major source of descending projections to the medullary trigeminal subnucleus caudalis (Sp5C), a region that plays a pivotal role in migraine pathophysiology.

paraventricual hypothalamic neurons project to the superior salviary nucleus, a region which is part of the parasympathethic autonomic outflow to cephaic and ocular structures and to laminae I-II of the trigeminal subnucleus caudalis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the neuroanatomical, neurochemical and electrophysiological properties of the hypothalamic control of the trigeminovascular system.
the study of the mechanisms underlying the control of the activity of trigeminovascular neurons.
the identification of hypothalamic circuitry that may be involved in the pathophysiological mechanisms of primary headaches.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PVN is a key structure for the control of trigeminovascular mechanisms involved in migraine and other primary headaches.

the PVN, a key brain structure for autonomic and neuroendocrine regulation, has a direct functional influence on the trigeminovascular system and that this influence may play a role in the generation of headaches.

the hypothalamus, and in particular the PVN, has a pivotal role in the pathophysiological processes of migraine and other headache disorders, and that the PVN is a key site of convergence for nociceptive, stress, and autonomic signals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the hypothalamus, and particularly the paraventricual nucleus, is involved in the pathophysiological processes underlying migraine and trigemino-autonomic cephalalgia.
hypothalamic PVN neurons directly control both basal and evoked activities in Sp5C neurons by modulating GABAergic, PACAPergic, and 5-HT1BDergic mechanisms.

the hypothalamus, via the paraventricual nucleus of the hypothalamic, controls the activities of the medullary trigeminal nucleus and that this control could be involved in the modulation of migraine and/or other trigeminal autononic cephalalgias.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the paraventricual nucleus of the hypothalamic (PVN) is a major player in the modulation of trigeminal pain.
the hypothalamus, through its projections to the Sp5C, could play a role in the pathophysiological processes of migraine and trigeminovascular headaches.
PVN neurons are in a position to modulate trigeminovascular activities and could be a therapeutic target for the treatment of migraine and other trigeminal autonimic cephalalgias.
